steps.sub: It sounds small — until the interviewer adds 'for a billion links and 100M reads a second.' By the end of this you'll have the HLD frame in your pocket: clarify, estimate, then reach for caching, the right database, load balancing — and explain the CAP tradeoff without sweating.

steps.prompt: Interviewer: 'design Twitter's feed.' What do you do BEFORE drawing a single box?

options.t: Draw the whole architecture from memory as fast as possible.
Clarify functional + non-functional requirements, then ESTIMATE the scale — reads/sec, writes/sec, storage.
Pick a database and start there.

steps.why: Every strong HLD answer opens the same way: nail the requirements (what must it do? how fast? how available?), then do back-of-envelope math — 'say 100M daily users, ~10 reads each = ~1B reads/day ≈ ~12K reads/sec.' Those numbers DRIVE every later decision. Drawing boxes before estimating is the surest way to over- or under-build.
hints: Boxes are downstream of numbers. What must you know first?
The opening move is always: requirements, then a scale estimate.

steps.prompt: The HLD building blocks you'll wire together.
steps.sub: Tap each card — these five cover most system-design rounds.

cards.b: Sits in front, spreads traffic across servers. L4 = fast, transport-level (IP/port). L7 = smarter, reads the request (route by URL/header).
Keeps hot data in memory (Redis). Turns a 50ms DB read into a sub-ms hit. The cheapest way to 10× read latency.
The source of truth. SQL for structured + transactions; NoSQL for scale + flexible schema. Shard it when one box can't hold the data.
Decouples services. Producer drops a job, consumer picks it up later — absorbs spikes, lets things run async.
Caches static content (images, JS) at edge locations near users — cuts latency and offloads your origin servers.

steps.prompt: Your reads are hammering the database and latency is climbing. What's the cheapest fix that buys the biggest win?
steps.sub: This is the move interviewers expect you to reach for instantly.

options.t: Buy a much bigger database server.
Add a cache (e.g. Redis) in front for hot reads — most requests hit memory, the DB only sees misses.
Rewrite the app in a faster language.

steps.why: Caching is the highest-leverage move for read-heavy systems. A read-through / cache-aside layer absorbs the popular queries in memory, so the DB load drops dramatically and latency goes sub-millisecond on hits. You then mention an eviction policy (LRU/LFU) and how you handle stale data — that depth is what scores.
hints: Read-heavy + slow DB → what layer sits between app and DB?
It keeps hot data in memory so most reads never touch the database.

steps.prompt: SQL or NoSQL? Sort each requirement by what it pushes you toward.
steps.sub: Tap an item, then a bin. The deciding question: do you need transactions + structure, or scale + flexibility?

items.t: bank transfers that must never lose money (ACID transactions)
a billion flexible, ever-changing user-activity events
strong relationships + complex JOINs across tables
massive horizontal scale across many cheap nodes
a strict, well-known schema that rarely changes
a schema that varies per document and evolves fast

hints: Need ACID, JOINs, a fixed schema? That's classic SQL territory.
Need to scale out horizontally with flexible, changing data? NoSQL.

steps.prompt: CAP — the tradeoff you'll be asked to defend.
steps.sub: Tap each card. The trick: CAP only bites DURING a network partition.

cards.b: Every read sees the latest write. All nodes agree right now.
Every request gets a (non-error) response, even if it might be slightly stale.
The system keeps working when the network splits nodes apart. On a distributed system, partitions WILL happen — so P is non-negotiable.
Since P is forced, the actual decision under a partition is C vs A. Banking → pick C. Social feed → pick A (a slightly stale tweet is fine).

steps.sub: Tap True or False for each, then check.

statements.t: You can have all three of Consistency, Availability, and Partition tolerance at the same time.
statements.why: No — CAP says pick 2 of 3. In a distributed system partitions are unavoidable (P is forced), so the genuine choice under a partition is C vs A.

statements.t: Estimating QPS and storage early helps you justify every later design choice.
statements.why: Right — the numbers tell you whether you need sharding, how big the cache should be, how many servers. Estimation is the backbone of a credible HLD answer.
Mostly no — caches primarily speed up READS. Writes still go to the source of truth, and you must decide write-through vs write-back and how to invalidate stale cache entries.

statements.t: An L7 load balancer can route requests based on the URL path or headers.
statements.why: Yes — L7 operates at the application layer, so it can read the request and route '/images/*' to one pool and '/api/*' to another. L4 only sees IP/port.

hints: CAP forces a choice — you don't get all three.
Caches help the read path; writes are a separate concern.

steps.prompt: Design the URL shortener live. Make each call as the interviewer probes.
steps.sub: Goal stays on screen. Pick the move that shows HLD judgment.
steps.goal: Shorten 1B URLs; handle 100M redirects/sec, mostly reads.

options: Clarify scope + estimate: read:write ratio, storage for 1B URLs
turns.log: 📐 Estimate → heavy reads, ~100:1 read:write, ~ a few TB storage.

turns.situation: Reads massively outnumber writes. The DB alone can't take 100M reads/sec.
turns.q: What do you add to the read path?
options: A cache (Redis) for hot short-codes, in front of the DB
Nothing — let the DB handle it
turns.log: ⚡ Cache layer → most redirects served from memory.

turns.situation: Traffic comes from one big region; one app server is saturating.
turns.q: What sits in front of your app servers?
options: A load balancer spreading traffic across many servers
A second copy of the database only
turns.log: ⚖️ Load balancer → traffic spread across the fleet.

turns.situation: Interviewer: 'a network partition hits between data centers. Stale redirect or downtime?'
turns.q: What's your CAP call here, and why?
options: Favour Availability — a slightly stale redirect beats a dead link
Favour Consistency and return errors during the partition
Refuse to answer — CAP is theoretical
turns.log: ✅ Chose A over C: a stale-but-working redirect is the right tradeoff for this product.

hints: Numbers first, then cache, then load balancing, then defend the CAP call.
For a redirect service, 'always works, maybe slightly stale' beats 'down'.

steps.prompt: AI drafts you a full HLD diagram in one shot. What's the operator's job under interview pressure?
steps.sub: The agent can draw boxes. It can't own the tradeoffs.

options.t: Read the diagram back word for word — it's already complete.
Pressure-test it: do the estimates support this? where's the bottleneck? what's the CAP call? — and defend each choice as YOUR reasoning.
Add every component you can think of to look thorough.

steps.why: AI gives you a plausible diagram; it doesn't give you judgment. The interviewer is testing whether YOU understand why each box is there, where it breaks at scale, and which tradeoffs you accepted. Your value is the reasoning — stress-test the agent's draft against the numbers and own the answer.
hints: A diagram isn't an argument. What does the interviewer actually grade?
Every box needs a 'because the estimate says…' behind it.

steps.sub: Not graded. Tie HLD to the role you want.

fields.label: Pick a product you'd love to reverse-engineer as HLD practice:
fields.ph: e.g. WhatsApp, Uber, YouTube, a ticket-booking site

fields.label: Which HLD building block do you most want to get fluent in first?
fields.ph: e.g. caching, sharding databases, the CAP tradeoff, load balancing
